paragraphs: Mikkelal abot melakot hannehugot etzel haadam tamid hi meleket hattochen, veyesh lah toladot harbeh shehem metzuyim lipne haadam veoseq bahem bime hachol; ulekak tzarik lo zekira gedola shello yishkach veyaabor alehem. v"g dimleket hattechina, iqqarah hi bitbua veqitniyyot, im kol zeh, kol giddule-qarqa, perot viraqot shehem okel gamur, yesh bahem issur tochen, hoil veyesh bemino techina, dehaynu sheyyesh bitbua veqitniyyot shehem gam ken giddule-qarqa. lepikak asur lachtok hayyaraq daq daq, veken asur lachtok gerogarot vecharubin daq daq baabur hazzeqenim, deim chatekem daq daq, yesh bazeh issur tochen; abal muttar liprer hallechem daq daq lipne hattarnegolim veopot shebbabbayit shemmezunnotam al haadam, hoil denitchana hattebua qodem asiyyat hallechem, deen techina achar techina.

clarification.explanation: One of the most common Sabbath labors is the labor of grinding, which has many derivatives that a person encounters in daily life, and therefore special care is needed not to transgress them by mistake. Although the main prohibition of grinding concerns grain and legumes, vegetables and fruits that are "produce of the ground" (grown from the earth) also carry the prohibition of grinding, since their kind can be ground (grain and legumes are also produce of the ground). Therefore it is forbidden to cut vegetables into very fine pieces, and it is likewise forbidden to cut dried figs and carobs into very fine pieces (for the elderly, for whom chewing is difficult), since such fine cutting is considered grinding. But it is permitted to crumble bread into very fine pieces for chickens and fowl, since the grain has already been ground in the process of making the bread, and there is no "grinding after grinding."
takeaways: It is forbidden to cut fresh vegetables and fruits (produce of the ground) into very fine pieces on the Sabbath, out of concern for the prohibition of grinding, but it is permitted to crumble bread (already ground) for animals.

paragraphs: Yesh omerim deen issur lachtok perot viraqot daq daq, ella bechotek umannicha lisuda acheret libbo bayyom, abal im okel lealtar o tok shaa achat, muttar lachtok daq daq, ukemo shekkatabti bedin habborer. veyesh machmirin leesor lachtok daq daq bekol gavna apillu leekol lealtar. ubemaqom shennahagu hetter, en limchot beyadam; veraq tzarik lehazhiram shello yaasu ken ella leekol lealtar o lisuda shehi semuka tok shaa achat. upoh irenu bagdad nohagim hetter lachtok daq daq, sheosin "tzalata" mipperot viraqot beshabbat, vetzarik lehazhiram shello yaasu letzorek seuda acheret shehi achar shaa achat.

clarification.explanation: Some say the prohibition of cutting fruits and vegetables into very fine pieces applies specifically when cutting and setting aside for a later meal that same day, but if eating immediately or within an hour — it is permitted to cut them very fine (similar to the law of sorting). Others are stringent and forbid it in every case, even for immediate eating. Where the lenient practice is followed, one should not protest, but people should be warned to do so only for immediate eating or within an hour. In Rabbi Yosef Chaim's city (Baghdad) the lenient practice was followed regarding preparing a salad ("salata") from fruits and vegetables on the Sabbath, but people should be warned not to do this for a meal more than an hour later.
takeaways: Cutting fruits and vegetables very fine on the Sabbath is permitted (according to the lenient view) only for immediate eating or within an hour, not for a later meal.

paragraphs: En issur tochen noheg ella begiddule-qarqa, abal basar mebushshal o tzali, o gebina vekayyotze bahem sheenam giddule-qarqa, muttar lachtok daq daq letzorek oto hayyom, vaapillu babboqer letzorek seudat ben-haarbayim. umihu, asur ligror haggebina bemorag charutz hamyuchad lah bime hachol apillu leekol miyyad, demecheze oseh keobadin dechol, veod dehave kishchiqat sammanim bemakteshet shellahem; ella yegarerenna besakkin vekayyotze, dela have derek chol.

clarification.explanation: The prohibition of grinding applies only to produce of the ground, but cooked or roasted meat, cheese, and similar items that are not produce of the ground — may be cut very fine for eating that same day, even in the morning for the afternoon meal (the later meal, toward sunset). Nevertheless, it is forbidden to grate cheese with a grater designated for that purpose during the week, even if one wishes to eat immediately, since this appears as an ordinary weekday act, and additionally resembles grinding spices in a vessel designated for that purpose — rather one should grate it with a knife or similar implement, which is not considered the weekday manner.
takeaways: It is permitted to cut meat, cheese, and similar foods (not produce of the ground) very fine for eating that same day, but cheese should not be grated with the grater designated for that purpose — a plain knife should be used instead.

paragraphs: En laduk happilpelin bemakteshet kelal, ella yaduk otam biqara, ubeqatta desakkina, dehave tere shinnuyim. veyizzaher shettihyeh haqqeara aba shello tishshaber, mippene shehappilpelin qashim hem. vehammelach dino kepilpelin detzarik shene shinnuyim, vela saggi beshinnuy echad, ukemo shekkatab "olat-shabbat" v"eliyya rabba" v"matteh-yeuddeh" za"l; vahagam ki haggaon rabbenu eliyyahu mivvilena za"l bisip qatan t' sebira lah lechalleq ben melach lepilpelin - berarti bs"d bsh"q "mqbtzl" dehaiqqar hu kaasher hebinu harabbanim za"l hannizkarim bekavvanat mera"n za"l, sheddin hammelach hu shaveh ledin happilpelin.

clarification.explanation: One should not pound pepper in a mortar at all on the Sabbath, but rather pound it in a bowl using the handle of a knife — these being two variations; and one should be careful that the bowl be thick so it does not break, since pepper is hard. And salt has the same law as pepper, requiring two variations and not sufficing with just one (Olat Shabbat, Eliyah Rabbah, Matteh Yehuda). And although the Vilna Gaon distinguished between salt and pepper, the Ben Ish Chai (in Miqabtzeel) determined that the primary view, as the aforementioned rabbis understood Maran's intent, is that the law of salt is the same as the law of pepper.
takeaways: On the Sabbath one does not pound pepper in a mortar, but rather in a bowl (thick) with the handle of a knife — two variations.
Salt has the same law as pepper — it requires two variations (not like the Vilna Gaon, who distinguished between them).

paragraphs: Gerogarot vecharubin ushear perot, dinam kemelach debaenan tere shinnuyim vela saggi beshinnuy echad, shekken mashma middibre hattosepta deshabbat (tv, yg) ubetza (, yg) shehebiah harab hammaggid za"l bepereq k" mehilkot shabbat, din g', ayyen sham; veken heela mori harab za"l, vehaemet atu bazeh, deken nireh lekol meayyen yashar deen lechalleq benehem, vekaasher katabti bsh"q "mqbtzl". veda, ki poh irenu bagdad y" nohagim laduk temarim veegozim veluzim vaapunim qeluyim bemakteshet sheddakin bah bechol, veraq osim shinnuy qetzat lahapok yad hammakteshet laduk berosh haddaq velo berosh harachab. ulepi haamur leel, gam bishar perot baenan tere shinnuyim, vekan en osim ella shinnuy echad, lahapok yad hammakteshet; veal zeh epshar lomar denahagu kisbarat "haagur" veshibbole halleqet disbira lehu desaggi beshinnuy echad, beram da aqa, ki en hashshinnuy haechad hazzeh hu shinnuy gamur, ki beemet hem koteshim beyad hammakteshet shebbah koteshim bechol, veraq hem mehappekim otah laduk barosh hashsheni, umi yomar dezeh chashib shinnuy? vbsh"q "rab-pealim" hebeti reaya deeno moil shinnuy kazeh mimmah shekkatab mera"n za"l bet yosep, siman tqy"d, m"terumat-haddeshen" za"l, deshiyyure petila shekkabu beshabbat asur lehadliq beyom tob mishshum hakana, veasur apillu barosh hashsheni shello hudlaq attu rosh shehudlaq; venitbaer din zeh sham beorek, dehaggaon mahari"y iserelin sebira lehu davqa bidorayeta gazerinan, ubidrabbanan la gazerinan; verashi"y sebira lehu apillu bidrabbanan, im hu qarob levadday deyishtammesh bimqom haissur, ayyen sham. vahagam demera"n za"l hittir beshiyyure petila, haynu mittaam acher, disbira lah kerob happoseqim dela chashebi lazeh hakana, abal bedabar zeh degazeru ha attu ha, lo piqpeq mera"n za"l kelal. gam raa tireh bemahari"y iserelin za"l, dirayato hi middin hassakkin shel shechita, degazerinan tzad hayyapeh attu tzad happagum, yeuyyan sham. vechazarti veamarti sham deyesh lomar: kevan dela matzinu dabar zeh meporash bedin hammakteshet ligzor betzad haqqatzar attu tzad harachab - en lanu ledammot dabar zeh ledabar acher ligzor middatenu, ukemo shekkatab harab hammaggid za"l bepereq Adonai mehilkot chametz umatztza, halaka k', al chashashat haraaba"d, veken katab happeri chadash za"l behilkot happesach, siman tn", al dibre habbet chadash za"l, deen lilmod gezerot zo mizzo. amenam shub katabti dibniddon didan en anachnu baim leesor mishshum gezera, ella middina asur, deha gam lisbarat "haagur" veshibbole halleqet modo debaenan shinnuy gamur; venireh lekulle alema dehippuk yad hammakteshet, en zeh shinnuy gamur ella shinnuy qetzat. vehinneh techillat hakkol berarti: kol midi deasur min hattora, eno muttar lekattechilla ella beshinnuy gamur, veim oseh shinnuy qetzat, adayin zeh hu asur midderabbanan. vehinneh, middin hammolel melilot beshabbat sheppasaq mera"n za"l besiman shy"t deen molelin melilot ella molel beshinnuy meat berashe etzbeotayv - hokachti mizzeh degam kan, ketisha berosh haqqatzar have shinnuy; veod hokachti middin hahotzaa sheppasaq haramba"m behilkot shabbat, pereq y"b: hammotzi leachar yado o beraglo, bepiv ubemarpeqo veku', patur, abal asur middibre soperim; veayyen beshulchan aruk lehaggaon rabbenu zalman, siman sh", seip b', yeuyyan sham. venimtza degam hippuk hammakteshet dela nicha tashmisheh, chashib kilachar yad, veshinnuy qetzat hu, velaken bemelach dilkulle alema yesh issur tora bidyakketu, la mehanne hippuk yad hammakteshet, abal ketishat perot, deikka bazeh pelugta, deit disbira lehu dedikatam hu issur derabbanan, en limchot beyad ellu haosim shinnuy zeh behippuk yad hammakteshet, "g deberarnu deen zeh shinnuy gamur - meachar denahagu beshinnuy zeh, en limchot beyadam, ubiprat im osim letzorek zeqenim uqetannim. veshaalti meet harab haggaon rabbi eliyyahu manni nr"v al minhag are haqqodesh tvb"b bedabar zeh, veheshib sheshshama shekken nohagim beir haqqodesh yerushalayim t"v shemmehappekin rosh hammadok vedakin bo beshabbat kemo minhag bagdad y".

clarification.explanation:
Dried figs, carobs, and other fruits that one wishes to pound on the Sabbath — have the same law as salt, requiring two variations, with one variation not sufficing; this is implied by the Tosefta in Shabbat and Beitzah brought by the Maggid, and Rabbi Yosef Chaim's teacher likewise concluded this — and the truth is with him, that there is no reason to distinguish between them, as he wrote in his book Miqabtzeel.

Rabbi Yosef Chaim relates that in his city of Baghdad it was customary to pound dates, walnuts, hazelnuts, and roasted chickpeas in the same mortar used for pounding during the week, only making a slight variation — turning the pestle's handle to pound with its narrow end rather than its wide end. According to what was said, other fruits too require two variations, and here there is only one; one could say the custom follows the view of the Agur and Shibbolei HaLeket that one variation suffices — except that the difficulty is that even this single variation is not a complete variation, since one pounds with the same weekday pestle and merely turns it — and who is to say this counts as a variation?

In his book Rav Pe'alim he brought proof that such a variation does not help: the Beit Yosef cited from Terumat HaDeshen that wick remnants that burned on the Sabbath may not be lit on a Festival due to "preparation," and this is forbidden even for the second end that was not lit — a decree due to the end that was lit. Maharai Isserlein holds that such a decree applies specifically to a Torah-level prohibition, while Rashi holds that it applies even to a rabbinic prohibition if it is nearly certain one will use the forbidden part. And although Maran permitted wick remnants — this was for a different reason, since he held, like most authorities, that this is not "preparation," but he did not at all question the basic decree of one end due to its counterpart; and Maharai Isserlein's proof comes from a slaughtering knife, where a decree is made on the good side due to the flawed side. Afterward he retracted and said: since we find no explicit decree regarding a mortar to decree the short side due to the wide side, we should not compare one thing to another and decree on our own, as the Maggid and Peri Chadash wrote that decrees are not derived from one another. Yet he again wrote that in this matter the concern is not due to a decree but from the letter of the law itself, since even the Agur and Shibbolei HaLeket agree that a complete variation is required, and by all accounts turning the pestle's handle is not a complete variation but only a slight one.

And at the outset he established a foundation: anything Torah-forbidden is permitted as the primary practice only with a complete variation, and one who makes only a slight variation is still rabbinically forbidden. And that pounding with the narrow end is nonetheless considered some variation, he proved from the law of rubbing grain kernels on the Sabbath — where Maran ruled that one may rub them only with a slight variation using the fingertips — and from the law of carrying, where the Rambam ruled: one who carries something out in an unusual manner, with his foot, mouth, or elbow, is exempt but rabbinically forbidden. It follows that turning the mortar, which is not convenient to use this way, is considered an unusual manner — a slight variation.

The conclusion: for salt, which by all accounts carries a Torah prohibition when pounded, turning the pestle's handle does not help; but for pounding fruits, which is disputed, with some holding its prohibition is only rabbinic — one should not protest against those who make this variation of turning the mortar, even though we determined it is not a complete variation, since this is already the accepted custom, especially when done for the sake of the elderly and children. And Rabbi Yosef Chaim asked the eminent Rabbi Eliyahu Mani about the custom in the Holy Cities, and he replied that he heard the same custom is followed in the Holy City of Jerusalem — turning the pestle's head and pounding with it on the Sabbath, as in the Baghdad custom.
takeaways: Pounding fruits on the Sabbath has the same law as salt — as the primary practice it requires two variations, not one.
Turning the pestle's handle to the narrow end is only a "slight variation," not a complete one.

For salt (a Torah prohibition by all accounts) the turning does not help; for fruits (where some hold it is only rabbinic) one should not protest against those who follow this practice, especially for the elderly and children.
This was the Baghdad custom, and Rabbi Eliyahu Mani testified that the same custom is followed in Jerusalem as well.

paragraphs: Tzeror yabesh asur leparero mishshum tochen, veken tit sheal habbeged, im hu yabesh asur legarero meal habbeged; veken asur leshapshep habbeged - ben mibbachutz, ben mibbipnim - kede lehaabir hattit mealayv, bipne shehattit hayyabesh mitparrer leperurim daqqim "y shipshup o gerira, vahare zeh toledet tochen.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to crumble a clump of dry earth, out of concern for grinding, and likewise it is forbidden to scrape dry mud off a garment, and it is also forbidden to rub the garment (from inside or outside) to remove the mud from it, since the dry mud crumbles into fine particles through rubbing or scraping, and this is a derivative of grinding.
takeaways: Dry mud on a garment may not be removed by scraping or rubbing on the Sabbath, since the resulting crumbling is considered a derivative of the labor of grinding.

paragraphs: Abaq hattoton (tabbaq haracha) sheshshoapin oto bachotem, velipamim yityabbesh bikli shello venaaseh kemo regabim medubbaqim, vei epshar lishop oto ella im ken meporarim oto daq daq - muttar lerasqo uletachanu ben etzbeotayv beshabbat, veen kan mishshum tochen, mippene dikbar nitchan miqqodem "y adam, veen tochen achar tochen; ak lo hittiru lerasqo "y keli, ella raq berashe etzbeotayv dehave shinnuy gamur. veayyen "mayim rabbim", orach chayyim, siman k"h, veod ayyen "qemach-solet", dap p"z, ammud g mah shekkatab beshem "bet- haroeh", ayyen sham. v"g demin harab "tal-orot", dap l"g, seip d' mashma demattir lishchaqu "y keli ad sheyyitparer - heeleti bsh"q "mqbtzl", haiqqar lishchaqu berashe etzbeotayv, dehave shinnuy gamur middarko bechol. umah shennistappeq harab magen abraham za"l sham besop debarayv bedibre mahari"l za"l: ulay lo ameru "en tochen achar tochen" ella baokalim - heeleti deen lehistappeq bekak, vaapillu ledidah shehu mistappeq bekak, yodeh deim marseqo berashe etzbeotayv let lan bah.

clarification.explanation: Snuff (tobacco powder for sniffing) that dries in its container and forms stuck-together clumps, which cannot be inhaled unless crumbled very fine — may be crushed and ground between the fingers on the Sabbath, since it was already ground earlier by a person (in the process of manufacturing the tobacco), and there is no "grinding after grinding." Nevertheless, it was not permitted to crush it with a vessel, only with the fingertips, since that is a complete variation from the weekday manner. The Magen Avraham, following the words of the Maharil, raised a doubt whether the rule "there is no grinding after grinding" applies specifically to foods and not to tobacco, which is not food — but Rabbi Yosef Chaim determined there is no room for this doubt, and in any case even one who entertains this doubt would agree that when crushing with the fingertips (a complete variation from the weekday manner), it is permitted according to all views.
takeaways: It is permitted to crumble dry snuff between the fingertips on the Sabbath (since it was already ground before), but not with the help of a vessel — only by hand and with a variation from the weekday manner.

Even according to the view that entertains doubt whether "no grinding after grinding" applies specifically to foods and not to tobacco, all agree that crushing with the fingertips (a complete variation) is permitted according to all views.

paragraphs: Muttar liqtom apillu besakkin qash o teben lachatzotz bo shinnayv, mippene deqash veteben hem akele behema, vekol dabar haomed laakila, mukan hu lekol hatztzorek, abal qesam sheeno maakal behema - apillu litlo kede lachatzotz bo shinnayv asur, vekannizkar besiman shk"b; vaapillu beyom tob shehu rauy lehassaqa, apillu hake asur lachtzotz bo shinnayv, ukemo shekkatab harab "shulchan-atze-shittim" za"l, dibyom tob lo nittenu etzim ella lehassaqa; vaapillu etz yabesh, en mishtammeshin bo ella letzorek hassaqa velo letzorek acher, dekol dabar sheeno keli, asur letaltelo apillu letzorek gupo; veayyen mg", siman tq"b, seip qatan y" vy"b veod acharonim sham. veha deasarnu lachtzotz shinnayv beqesam apillu belo qetima, haynu im lo tiqqenu vehekinu meereb-shabbat lekak, abal im tiqqenu vehekinu lekak meereb shabbat, muttar lachtzotz bo shinnayv meachar daasao keli.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to pick between the teeth with straw or hay, and even to cut them with a knife for this purpose, since they are animal fodder — and anything intended for eating is ready for any use. But a wood splinter that is not animal fodder — even handling it in order to pick teeth is forbidden. Even on a Festival, when wood is permitted for kindling, it is nevertheless forbidden to use a splinter to pick teeth, since on a Festival wood was permitted only for the purpose of kindling and not for another purpose, and anything that is not a vessel is forbidden to handle even for its own use. If a special splinter was prepared and fashioned before the Sabbath for the purpose of picking teeth — it thereby becomes a "vessel," and it is permitted to use it.
takeaways: It is permitted to pick teeth with straw or hay (animal fodder), but an ordinary splinter is forbidden for this use unless specially prepared beforehand on the Sabbath eve.

paragraphs: Atze besamim, "g demuttar lachtzotz bahem shinnayv - asur liqtom otam beyadayv lachtzotz bahem shinnayv; veayyen "eshel- abraham", siman shk"b v"chayye-adam", kelal m"d, ot y"ch ushear acharonim; abal im rotzeh leharicha baatze besamim, muttar limlol veliqtom otam beyadayv leharicha bahem - echad qashim, veechad rakkim; mihu, lo hittiru liqtom besakkin ella bayyad ukemo shekkatab rsh"l za"l, vehiskimu ken haacharonim, vedachu dibre hatta"z shehittir apillu bikli; mihu gam rsh"l lo asar liqtom besakkin ella beqashim, abal birkayim muttar liqtom gam besakkin, vekannizkar b"eliyya raba" umishbetzot zahab ushear acharonim za"l. gam hittiru liqtom baatze besamim ellu kede litten lachabero leharicha, udelo k"sheyare keneset haggedola" deasar bazeh; veayyen leharab machaziq beraka, siman shk"b, ot g', v"zekor leabraham", cheleq g, dap m"z, veken hamminhag pashut, vehammachmir bazeh, tabo alayv beraka.

clarification.explanation: Aromatic wood — although it is permitted to pick teeth with it — it is forbidden to break it by hand in order to pick teeth with it. But if one wants to smell aromatic wood, it is permitted to crush and break it by hand for the purpose of smelling, whether it is hard or soft. It was permitted to break it with a knife only when done by hand, and this specifically for hard wood; but for soft wood it is permitted to break it even with a knife. It was likewise permitted to break aromatic wood also in order to let a friend smell it, contrary to a more stringent opinion.
takeaways: It is permitted to break aromatic wood by hand (and soft wood also with a knife) for the purpose of smelling — even for another person — but not for the purpose of picking teeth.

paragraphs: Eged shel hadas ushear mine besamim shehu asuy min lulebe temarim - la mibbaaya beod hahadas agud bo demuttar lachtzotz shinnayv berashim shello, ella gam achar shehuttar min hahadas, shennishar haeged lebaddo, gam ken muttar lachtzotz bo shinnayv, daadayin torat keli alayv, deepshar leegod bo hadas vaatze besamim beqesher hammuttar beshabbat. vezeh davqa beodo lach, abal im nityabbesh, deen rauy leegod bo, vehu eno maakal behema, asur lachtzotz bo shinnayv, dedino kaqqesam shetztzarik lihyot metuqqan umukan mibbeod yom lekak.

clarification.explanation: A bundle (tied bunch) of myrtle and other aromatic herbs made from palm-frond stems — it is permitted to pick teeth with its ends while it is still tied together with the myrtle, and even after the myrtle has been removed and only the bundle remains, it is still permitted to pick teeth with it, since it still has the status of a "vessel" (it can be used again to tie other myrtle branches, with a knot permitted on the Sabbath). This applies specifically while it is still moist; but if it has dried out to the point of being unfit for tying, and it is not animal fodder — it is forbidden to pick teeth with it, having the law of an ordinary splinter that requires advance preparation.
takeaways: A moist myrtle bundle (still fit for use as a "vessel") may be used to pick teeth, but once dried and no longer fit for use, it has the law of an ordinary splinter, which is forbidden.

paragraphs: Poh irenu bagdad darkam laasot menipa sheqqorin "merevacha" (menipa meale lulab) shemmenipin bah lishob rucha, veosim millulabim shel temarim sheenam reuyim lemaakal behema, vekaasher teballeh zot hammenipa, yukal haadam lachtzotz bah shinnayv berashe haqqesamim hayyotzeim mimmenna beodam mechubbarim bah, veen tzorek liqtom otam kelal, umuttar zeh beshabbat; deellu haqqesamim shehu chotzetz shinnayv berashehem odam mechubbarim bikli hammenipa hazzeh veyesh torat keli alehem. veraq yizzaher lachtzotz benachat shello yishtabberu, deim yaaseh bekoach vechozeq, yishtabberu bevadday vehave pesiq resheh. vedomeh lazeh matzinu besiman shl"z, seip b, behaggahat hashshulchan, deasur lekabbed habbegadim "y makbedot haasuyim miqqesamim, shello yishtabberu qesemehem; veayyen magen abraham v"machatzit-hashsheqel", ayyen sham. veayyen "shulchan-atze-shittim" bedine hammuqtzeh, bedin shibre keli-cheres, dedores alehen veeno choshesh, shekkatab sham babbeurim dechashub dabar sheeno mitkavven, ukemo deshare lelek al gab asabim beshabbat veku'. v"g deqayma lan deasur lekabbed habbegadim bammakbedot haasuyin miqqesamim, shello yishtabberu qesemehen - shane hatam deshober keli beyadayim, abal haka have mimmela, ayyen sham. vbsh"q "mqbtzl" katabti bs"d bazeh.

clarification.explanation: In Rabbi Yosef Chaim's city (Baghdad) it was customary to make a fan from palm-frond leaves ("marwaha"), and since palm fronds are not animal fodder — once the fan is worn out, it is permitted to pick teeth with the ends of the splinters protruding from it while they are still attached to it, without needing to break them off at all, since they are still part of the vessel. One should be careful to pick gently, so they do not break — for if done forcefully they would certainly break (which would be an "inevitable certain result," forbidden). Although it is known that it is forbidden to clean garments with a broom made of splinters, out of concern that its splinters might break, the leniency here is different: there, the person actually and intentionally breaks the splinter by hand while cleaning, whereas here the breaking of the splinter's end while picking teeth with it happens incidentally as a byproduct and not through a direct act of breaking, and therefore the law here is more lenient.
takeaways: It is permitted to pick teeth with the ends of the splinters of a worn-out palm-frond fan, as long as they are still attached to the vessel, provided one does so gently so they do not break.

The leniency here differs from the prohibition of cleaning garments with a splinter broom (where the splinter is broken by hand and intentionally) — here the breaking happens incidentally as a byproduct, and is therefore more lenient.

paragraphs: Im yesh lo qesam metuqqan umukan mibbeod yom lachtzotz bo shinnayv, "p sheeno rauy libhema - heeleti bsh"q "mqbtzl", deim oto qesam hu qal meod veyabesh, devadday mishtabber rosho bachatzitzat shinnayv im yachtzotz bekoach vechozeq, let lan bah, veen mechayyebin oto lachtzotz benachat "g dehave pesiq resheh, yaan ki zeh meqalqel hu, vehamqalqel bipsiqat hattalush, hare zeh muttar legamre, ukemo shekkatab haggaon magen abraham za"l, siman shy"ch, seip qatan l"v, veayyen acharonim sham, veayyen "shulchan-atze-shittim", bedin makkeh bepattish, ot b', yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: If there is a splinter prepared beforehand for picking teeth, and even though it is not animal fodder, that splinter is very light and dry such that its tip will certainly break if used forcefully to pick teeth — there is no problem with this, and there is no obligation to pick gently (even though this is a certain result of breakage), since breaking the splinter is "destructive" (an act of destruction rather than construction) performed on a cutting of a detached object, and such a destructive act is entirely permitted.
takeaways: A splinter prepared in advance for picking teeth may be used forcefully even if it breaks, since its breakage is considered "destructive," which is permitted on the Sabbath.

paragraphs: Mechattekin deluin lipne habbehema heka dehem qashim, sheen reuyim leakelam belo chittuk, ak yizzaher shello yechatek daq daq. vehambaqqea etzim, issuro mishshum ubda dechol, abal im chatako daq daq, chayyab mishshum tochen; veayyen magen abraham, siman tq"; veayyen "shulchan-atze-shittim", bedin makkeh bepattish, ot b', yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to cut a hard squash for an animal, when it is not fit to eat without cutting, but one must be careful not to cut it into very fine pieces. One who splits wood — his prohibition is only under the category of "weekday-like acts," but if he cuts it into very fine pieces, he is liable under the category of grinding.
takeaways: It is permitted to cut a hard squash for an animal into large pieces (not very fine); splitting wood is forbidden as a weekday-like act, and cutting it into very fine pieces is more severe — forbidden as grinding.

paragraphs: Hallash shiur gerogeret, chayyab min hattora, upachot mishshiur zeh, asur kedin chatzi shiur deasur min hattora. vehamgabbel et heapar o et haqqemach hare zeh toledet lash; veim lo gibbel ella raq natan mayim bilbad: yesh omerim, gam bazeh chayyab min hattora, veyesh omerim deasur bazeh midderabbanan; mihu, hammursan - "g deasur ligbul oto libhema o letarnegolim, yesh mattirin latet bo mayim, umaabir bo tarvad o maqqel sheti vaereb, kevan deeno memares beyado veeno mesabbeb hattarvad; veken hittiru name lenaaro mikkeli el keli kede sheyyitareb. veyesh oserin litten mayim al gab hammursan beshabbat kelal. uleinyan dina: "g demaran za"l satam kehammattirin, mikkol maqom yesh lachush ledaat haoserin bemursan shel irenu bagdad y", sheanachnu roin bo taarobet qemach beayin; veayyen "shiyyure-beraka" siman shk"d, mah shekkatab beshem mahari"y veelay za"l, veayyen "chesed laalapim" ushear acharonim.

clarification.explanation: One who kneads a dough of the volume of a dried fig is Torah-liable, and less than this measure is forbidden under the rule of "half the measure," which is Torah-forbidden. One who mixes earth or flour together — this is a derivative of the labor of kneading. If one only added water without mixing — some say one is Torah-liable even for this, and some say it is only rabbinically forbidden. Regarding bran — although it is forbidden to mix it for an animal or chickens, some permit adding water to it and stirring it with a stick in a criss-cross motion (without stirring by hand and without rotating the stick), and it was likewise permitted to shake it from vessel to vessel to mix it. There is a stricter opinion forbidding adding water to bran in any case. As halacha, although most authorities are lenient, one should be concerned for the stricter opinion regarding the bran of Rabbi Yosef Chaim's city, since in it one visibly sees an actual mixture of flour.
takeaways: Mixing flour or earth with water is Torah-forbidden at the measure of a dried fig; bran (coarse grain husks) may be mixed with water using a stick (not by hand) — but if it visibly contains significant flour, one should be stringent.

paragraphs: Abaq hattutin keshehu yabesh, asur litten alayv mayim ulegabelu beyadayim, dedame lemursan, sheggam maran za"l shessatam kehammattirin, eno ella latet bo mayim, abal legabbelo beyadayim lekulle alema asur. uminhag irenu bagdad y" lehannicha beshabbat tippot mayim bikli haqqatan shel abaq hattutin, vesogerim hakkeli, umakkim bikli al kap yadam kamma peamim kede sheyyithappek haabaq betoko veyitgabbel minneh ubeh, sheyyitarebu tippot hammayim bekullo vituqqan bekak; vedame zeh lamma shehittiru lenaer hammursan mikkeli el keli.

clarification.explanation: Dry snuff — it is forbidden to add water to it and knead it by hand, since this resembles the law of bran, where even the leniency (according to the lenient view) is only to add water and not to actually knead by hand — kneading by hand is forbidden according to all. In Rabbi Yosef Chaim's city (Baghdad) it was customary on the Sabbath to place drops of water in the small snuff container, close the container, and strike it with the palm of the hand several times so the powder mixes on its own and the water drops spread throughout it — this resembles the leniency of shaking bran from vessel to vessel to mix it.
takeaways: Snuff may not be kneaded by hand with water, but it is permitted to place water in a closed container and shake it (striking with the palm) to mix the water into the powder, similar to the leniency regarding bran.

paragraphs: En mashtinim beapar mishshum gibbul, veen mashtinim betit apillu shehu qasheh, mippene shennimmocha veyesh bazeh gibbul; v"g deeno mitkavven - pesiq resheh hu; veayyen magen abraham, siman shk", seip qatan y"t, v"machatzit-hashsheqel" sham; veayyen "eliyya raba" sham. vekatebu harab "eshel-abraham" veharab "tosepet shabbat", seip qatan l': "g derabbi yose berabbi yehuda sebira lehu eno chayyab ad sheyyegabbel, mikkol maqom issura ikka im en lo tzorek bazeh, ayyen sham. vekatabti bsh"q "mqbtzl", deim hu bammidbar dekol haqqarqa hu apar tachucha, vehutzrak lehashtin, muttar lehashtin veeno choshesh, dedame leha deaseru lehashtin besheleg, veim kol zeh hittiru lehashtin bemaqom shekkol haaretz melea sheleg, dekol kehay gavna shei epshar, lo gazeru chakamim.

clarification.explanation: One should not urinate on earth, due to the prohibition of kneading, and one should also not urinate on hard mud, since it dissolves from the urine and kneading results — and this is forbidden even though the person does not intend it, since this is a certain result ("an inevitable certain result"). The authors of "Eshel Avraham" and "Tosefet Shabbat" added: even though according to Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehuda there is no Torah liability for kneading earth through urination until it is actually kneaded by hand, nevertheless there is a prohibition (rabbinic) when the person has no need for the matter. Nevertheless, if one is in a desert where all the ground is loose earth, and is compelled to urinate — he may urinate there without concern, similar to the leniency to urinate on snow in a place where the entire ground is covered with snow — since in cases where there is no other option, the Sages did not decree.
takeaways: It is forbidden to urinate on earth or mud (which creates kneading), but in a desert where all the ground is loose earth and there is no other option — one may urinate there.

Even according to the lenient view (Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehuda) that there is no Torah liability for urinating on earth until it is actually kneaded, there is nevertheless a rabbinic prohibition when there is no need for it.

paragraphs: Im mekasseh me-raglayim bechol o eper hammukan lekak, yizzaher latet harbeh chol o eper, yaan deellu tiban - im yitten mehem meat, yitarebu beme-raglayim vehave gibbul; veim yitten harbeh, eno nikkar, vekannizkar b"chayye-adam", kelal y"t seip k', yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: One who covers urine with sand or ash designated for that purpose must be careful to use a large quantity of sand or ash, since if he uses only a little — it will mix with the urine and this will be forbidden kneading; if he uses a lot — the mixture will not appear as kneading.
takeaways: When covering urine with sand or ash on the Sabbath, one must use a large quantity, so the mixture is not considered forbidden kneading.

paragraphs: Hannoten zera pishtan o mah sheqqorin bearbe "bezar richan" (gerigere zera rechaniyyim) vekayyotze bemayim, yesh bazeh issur lash, vechayyab tekep mishsheyyittenem bemayim. veasur litten mayim o chometz letok chardal o shumin ketushim im oseh ballayla aba, de"g deen gibbul bekak, mikkol maqom nireh kelash; abal belila rakka, muttar, veraq yizzaher laasot "y shinnuy, shennoten hashshum o hachardal techilla vech"k hachometz; velo yeareb bekap ella beyado. ubemaqom sheddarkan bechol latet haokel techilla, yaaseh beshabbat lehepek vekannizkar baacharonim. v"tzelatah" sheosin miqqishshuin o shear perot viraqot, kevan deen chotekim otam daq daq lo shayyak behu gibbul umuttar laasotam ballayla aba veen tzarik shinnuy. v"g dehammagen abraham za"l hechmir lehatzrik belila rakka veshinnuy, haiqqar kemo shekkatab hatta"z, veken hiskim "eliyya raba" vetosepet shabbat ushear acharonim, veken hamminhag pashut.

clarification.explanation: One who puts flaxseed or similar aromatic seeds in water — this carries the prohibition of kneading, and he is liable immediately upon placing them in water. It is forbidden to add water or vinegar to mustard or crushed garlic if this creates a thick mixture, since even though this is not actual kneading, it appears like kneading. But with a soft mixture — it is permitted, provided one makes a variation from the normal order of operations used during the week (for example, if it is customary to first add the liquid and then the solid, on the Sabbath one should do the reverse), and should mix by hand rather than with a spoon. A salad ("salata") of squash and other fruits and vegetables — since they are not cut very fine, there is no concern of kneading in them, and it is permitted to prepare them as a thick mixture without any need for variation at all. And although the Magen Avraham was stringent, requiring a soft mixture and a variation here as well — the primary view follows the Taz, and so "Eliyah Rabbah" and "Tosefet Shabbat" and the other later authorities agreed, as is the plain custom.
takeaways: Preparing mustard or garlic with a liquid as a soft mixture is permitted with a variation in the order of operations; a thick mixture should be avoided entirely, except for a vegetable salad, which carries no concern of kneading at all.

paragraphs: Charoset sheosin bepesach, shemmannichim egozim shechuqim letok haddebash - im chal pesach beshabbat velo natan haegozim miqqodem, yitten beshabbat "y shinnuy sheyyitten haegozim techilla vech"k haddebash, mippene ki darkenu bechol litten haddebash techilla, vaapillu im oseh belayla aba muttar, kevan shehu letzorek mitzva; ken katab harab "shulchan-atze-shittim" umashma middebarayv deim eno oseh letzorek tibbul ella kede leekol, veken bishar shabbetot hashshana, tzarik lizzaher shello yaaseh ballayla aba; veken rauy lehorot laasot belila rakka v"y shinnuy.

clarification.explanation: Charoset made on Passover, in which crushed nuts are placed into honey — if Passover falls on the Sabbath and the nuts were not prepared in advance, it is permitted to prepare them on the Sabbath with a variation from the normal order of operations: putting the nuts first and the honey afterward (contrary to the normal weekday order, in which honey is put first) — even if the result is a thick mixture, since this is for the sake of a commandment (dipping at the Passover Seder). This differs from the other Sabbaths of the year, on which, absent a commandment need, one must be careful not to prepare a thick mixture, but only a soft one with a variation.
takeaways: Preparing charoset on the Sabbath (when Passover falls on the Sabbath) is permitted even as a thick mixture with a variation in order, since this is for the sake of a commandment — unlike preparing similar mixtures on ordinary Sabbaths, where only a soft mixture is permitted.
